articles.title: Congressional Briefing Uncovers Coordinated Russian Information Warfare Against Democrats
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox They said Moscow was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in three previous US elections. PHOTO: REUTERS Published Oct 22, 2026, 04:36 AM Updated Oct 22, 2026, 06:28 AM Set as preferred source Listen WASHINGTON – The top US Democratic lawmakers on the congressional intelligence committees on Oct 21 said they received an intelligence briefing that Russia has been waging a misinformation campaign against Democrats running in November’s midterm elections. The comments by Senator Mark Warner and Representative Jim Himes come as Republican President Donald Trump has in recent weeks eased economic sanctions on Russia and increased pressure on Ukraine to end its fight against Russian forces. Warner and Himes told reporters they were limited in revealing what they had learnt in an election security briefing that they had requested from Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton because it was classified. But, they said, Russia was waging the same kind of online misinformation campaign that the US intelligence community had tracked in US elections in 2016, 2020 and 2024. “And the state of play, I would argue, is that, you know, Russia, similar to prior occasions, is going after Democrats,” Warner said. He noted news reports that Democrat James Talarico, who is running for the US Senate in Texas, and Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election in Georgia, “in particular are being dinged” by fake advertisements created with artificial intelligence. The White House and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The Russian embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Moscow in the past has denied meddling in US elections. Himes said the pair could not provide details of the misinformation spread by Russia because the material was classified. But he added that Moscow’s conduct has been “the same old, same old”. “The Russians are kind of throwing everything out there,” said Himes. “Chaos, you know, don’t trust your voting machines.” He added there was “no reason to believe” that China has not been conducting “extremely targeted” efforts as it has done in the past to influence voters. The Chinese embassy did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Beijing has previously denied interfering in US elections. Recent Reuters/Ipsos polling has shown Democrats leading Republicans on the generic congressional ballot by high single digits to low double digits nationally, bolstering Democratic hopes of regaining control of the House of Representatives and possibly the Senate. The lawmakers said they were concerned that Trump could pursue efforts to contest election results, including by claiming foreign hacking of voting infrastructure. Himes emphasised that there was no evidence that any country could penetrate US election systems and change results. “Nothing out there suggests that there is even the capability or the intent to do interference, whereas there is a pretty robust influence environment,” said Himes. articles.title: Norway Eliminates Gaming and Messaging Exemptions from Social Media Limits
articles.content: Norway plans to apply its proposed social media age limit to platforms considered harmful to children, dropping earlier proposals to exempt messaging services and video games. The government has identified TikTok, Roblox and Snapchat as platforms that would be covered under the revised approach. The bill is expected to reach parliament by the end of 2026, although the government has not announced when the restrictions would take effect or what penalties would apply. What changed The proposed law previously included a list of exemptions, including messaging services and games, to avoid affecting harmless apps such as school communication tools. The government has now replaced this approach with a single condition: the law will apply only to social media platforms that pose a risk of harm to children. With this condition in place, blanket exemptions are no longer necessary and are being removed. Messaging services and games will not be categorically excluded; they will be covered if they meet the harm test. The government maintains that this change will not reduce the law’s scope. It argues that a risk-based test can identify harmful services, such as games with social media features, that a fixed list of exemptions might have missed. How “harmful” is defined The law defines a harmful social medium as one whose design, features or content create a risk to children’s emotional, cognitive or physical development or safety . The government says the law is intended to address several types of risk: Exposure to harmful content Addictive features Illegal marketing Unwanted contact from strangers Assessments of what constitutes harm will be based on current knowledge and updated as technology evolves. The government describes this as a more flexible approach, but its announcement does not specify who will conduct these assessments or how frequently they will take place. The age limit will apply until 1 January of the year in which a child turns 16. As written, this appears to mean that eligibility will be determined by birth year rather than the exact birthday, although the announcement does not explicitly clarify this. The proposed law has undergone consultation in Norway and across the wider European Economic Area (EEA). How it would be enforced The proposal is a national age-limit law that activates the enforcement and sanctioning obligations already contained in the EU’s Digital Services Act (DSA). In Norway, the DSA is to be implemented through a national Digital Services Act, which has undergone consultation but is not yet in force. The national law must come into force before enforcement can begin. Digitalisation Minister Torgeir Micaelsen said that implementing the law quickly is a high priority and will equip Norway to enforce the age limit on major platforms. He added that the government expects companies to comply immediately. Platforms will be responsible for choosing their own age-verification methods. These methods must be effective, privacy-friendly and compliant with the EU’s General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR). The government has not specified any particular technology. What the announcement does not say The announcement leaves several questions unanswered: No start date: The government has only stated that it intends to submit the bill by the end of 2026. No penalties specified: The announcement does not specify fines or other sanctions. No decision-maker identified: It does not say which authority will determine whether a platform is harmful or what procedure it will follow. Enforcement depends on another law: Enforcement relies on Norway’s national Digital Services Act, which has not yet been enacted. The government’s claim remains untested: The assertion that the risk-based test will not narrow the law’s scope reflects the government’s position. How games and messaging services will be treated in practice will depend on how the harm criteria are applied. articles.title: Homeland Security AI Inventory Exposes Federal Transparency Failures
articles.content: DHS’s AI Inventory Reveals the Limits of Federal AI Transparency Law and Eoghan Stafford Published on October 21, 2026 As immigration agents have carried out the Trump administration’s mass deportation campaign, they have used a range of AI-driven technologies – from facial recognition mobile apps to social media monitoring software – to locate individuals and to monitor peaceful protesters. While the administration has revealed few details about these technologies, some much-needed transparency could have come from the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) most recent AI use case inventory , published in January of this year ( with some revisions in June). By law, federal agencies must publish annual inventories of how they use artificial intelligence technologies (which the administration now calls super intelligence), and OMB guidance requires them to disclose how they manage the risks those technologies pose to people’s rights. As an examination of DHS’s current AI inventory reveals, however, the law has failed to ensure transparency. The information this administration requires its agencies to disclose about their use of AI is too limited to enable accountability, and DHS fails to meet even that minimal standard. Background The requirement for agencies to publish AI use-case inventories began with an executive order signed by President Trump in 2020. It was later codified into law in the Advancing American AI Act in 2022, which requires each agency to prepare, maintain, and publicly post an inventory of its AI use cases. President Biden’s Office of Management and Budget (OMB) issued a memo in 2024 that directed federal agencies to implement certain safeguards when using AI in ways that could significantly affect people’s rights or safety and required agencies to disclose how they had implemented those safeguards in their inventories. In April 2025, OMB rescinded and replaced the Biden-era memo on federal use of AI. While the 2025 OMB memo has many similarities to the 2024 version, it cut some crucial protections, such as the requirement that agencies measure and mitigate bias . More recently, DHS issued a directive on the use and acquisition of artificial intelligence that permits the chief AI officer to waive any departmental policy governing AI, including any prohibitions on uses; while the directive adds that waivers may not violate “law, regulation, and government-wide policy,” this authority creates an enormous loophole in the existing guidance. The inventories that DHS released during the Biden administration had their own transparency problems . Moreover, many of the concerning surveillance tools that Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) are using today have been in place for years . However, the costs of inadequate transparency are higher now, under an administration that seeks to arrest thousands of migrants a day while undermining efforts to hold federal agents accountable for abuses of power. How DHS Avoids Required Safeguards Under the 2025 OMB memo, agencies must report whether a given use of AI is “high-impact” in light of its potential effects on individuals’ rights or safety. The memo requires agencies to implement and disclose certain minimum safeguards for all high-impact AI use cases, including testing the system’s accuracy before deployment, auditing for misuse, and establishing a process to appeal decisions made using AI. An agency’s use of an AI tool is “high-impact” only if its outputs are “a principal basis” for an official action that affects someone’s rights or safety. As we have written previously, this standard, which the Biden-era memo also relied upon, is far too narrow . Agencies often consider many factors when making decisions, such as a determination by ICE or CBP agents to investigate or detain someone. If an AI’s recommendations, predictions, or other outputs influence such a consequential decision, then agents’ use of that AI should be subject to safeguards, whether or not the AI is a “principal” basis for the decision. Applying OMB’s narrow standard, DHS avoids implementing safeguards for many uses of AI that directly affect people’s rights. For example, the inventory does not classify the ELITE app as high-impact, although ICE agents use it to find and arrest migrants who may be in the country illegally. The app uses large language models to extract addresses where migrants may live from government records, including data from the Department of Health and Human Services , and displays them on maps, along with “confidence scores” indicating the likelihood that the addresses are accurate, facilitating widescale raids. DHS also excludes the Investigative Prioritization Aggregator software, which ranks suspects in criminal investigations by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a component of ICE, according to their likely importance to an investigation. Detaining or investigating people affects their rights by definition, and the risks are heightened under an administration that is not scrupulously abiding by its legal obligations and has carried out lethal military strikes of people on boats accused of smuggling drugs. Whether or not these AI systems provide a “principal basis” for decisions about whom to arrest or investigate, they directly shape those decisions. Similarly, the department determined that its use of Dataminr, a tool that scans social media and other public sources to “provide alerts for possible threats related to national security [and] border violence,” among other issues, was not high-impact, because the alerts just supply CBP officers with compiled information. This overlooks the substantial concerns associated with use of social media data, including the barriers to accurately decoding social media communications and the risk of inaccurately labeling someone a threat based on tainted, misinterpreted, or inadequately vetted data. DHS’s labels have consequences. Excluding technologies from the high-impact list allows DHS to skip safeguards—such as testing and auditing—making it easier for CBP or ICE to deploy technologies that are inaccurate or unreliable, increasing the risk of agents arresting innocent people. Wrongful arrest attempts can be deadly, as tragically underscored when, in two separate incidents during a single week in July, ICE agents killed Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Joan Sebastian Guerrero , after apparently confusing each of them with other individuals. Interactions with CBP officers can be high stakes as well, from searches of travelers’ electronic devices at the border to fatal encounters . Safeguards are also needed to prevent intentional misuse of AI systems, as detailed below. DHS Falls Short of the Agency’s Own Rules The 2025 OMB memo instructs agencies to presume that certain uses of AI are high-impact, and rightly includes activities such as identifying criminal suspects and assessing risks posed by individuals. In follow-up guidance released a few months after the memo, OMB further instructs agencies to explain any deviations from this list. However, DHS has not always done so. For example, although identifying criminal suspects is presumptively high-impact, DHS does not explain why the “AI-Enhanced ICE Tip Processing” system—which summarizes and ranks the urgency of tips submitted to ICE —is not listed as high-impact. This is not a harmless bureaucratic error. Determining which tips should be investigated determines which threats to public safety are prioritized, affecting the rights of individuals deemed to be suspects and potential crime victims alike. What the Inventory Doesn’t Say For high-impact uses of AI, the OMB memo requires agencies to implement certain measures to manage the technologies’ risks. ICE classifies six and CBP classifies 19 actively deployed use cases as high-impact, but the inventory reveals little about what safeguards are in place. OMB’s follow-up instructions on the AI inventories require agencies to answer nine questions about their compliance with the minimum safeguards for high-impact use cases. All but one of those questions are multiple choice, each with a list of three to six possible responses that convey very little. For example, CBP and ICE have deployed a high-impact facial recognition app called Mobile Fortify, which agents use to identify individuals they stop to question, potentially matching them to records in federal databases. This is indeed high-stakes technology. A false match could result in wrongful arrest or deportation. However, the agencies are not required to tell the public any meaningful details about their efforts to mitigate these risks. In answer to a question about whether they monitor the use of Mobile Fortify for harms to privacy, civil rights, or civil liberties, DHS simply selected a response that says: “Yes, sufficient monitoring protocols have been established.” This generic response is essentially useless, particularly in light of DHS’s removal of the only relevant policy from its website, along with reporting suggesting that ICE officials have told agents they can rely on Mobile Fortify results as “ definitive ” evidence of someone’s migration status and can ignore contrary evidence – even a birth certificate. The administration’s decision to stop requiring agencies to address demographic disparities in AI models compounds this problem, since facial recognition systems are generally less accurate on women and minorities. In addition, many of the questions that the Biden-era OMB instructions required agencies to answer were dropped from the Trump-era instructions, including: whether the AI use case has been tested in operational environments to understand its performance and potential impact on affected individuals or communities; whether a senior privacy official has assessed the privacy risks; whether the AI is used to significantly influence or inform decisions or actions that could have a negative impact on specific individuals or groups; and what steps the agency has taken to detect and mitigate significant disparities in performance across demographic groups. Excluding these kinds of granular questions deprives the public of important insights into how their government is using AI. Another gap in transparency stems from the fact that agencies are only legally required to release inventories annually, which allows them to deploy technologies in potentially harmful ways for months before the public learns much if anything about them. For instance, Mobile Fortify became operational at the start of May 2025, according to the inventory, but its existence would have remained a secret until January 2026 if 404 Media had not broken the story. As it was, the public did not learn key details , such as the company that developed the app, until the inventory was published; based on that information, WIRED reported that the app was not designed to confirm identities, as ICE agents are reportedly doing. If ICE agents deployed new AI surveillance tools during Operation Metro Surge in Minnesota in January 2026, the public might not learn about it until 2027. Similarly, recent reporting indicates that U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) is seeking to hire a contractor who will use artificial intelligence tools to help sift through mountains of governmental and commercial data as part of an effort to ramp up criminal investigations of fraud in immigration benefit applications. If the contract is awarded this year, an analysis of the impact of the tools and any risk mitigation efforts would be released in January 2027 at the earliest; if it is not awarded until next year, any disclosures are not likely to appear in the inventory until 2028. ICE’s Contradictory Use of Sentiment Analysis The inventory also reveals that ICE is violating its own policies on internet surveillance by employing automated sentiment analysis. An entry titled “Open-Source Intelligence for Investigations” reveals that HSI uses software systems that search online content for undefined “risks” and suggest “investigative leads.” These systems utilize sentiment analysis: AI methods for classifying the emotions or opinions expressed in text. The entry itself cites an official ICE policy that states the agency is prohibited from applying sentiment analysis technologies to online content during law enforcement investigations. The policy as written is right to ban sentiment analysis as a tool of criminal investigations. There is little reason to think that sentiment analysis systems could reliably identify real threats to public safety or legitimate criminal investigative leads, since AI models often misinterpret the tone or context of informal comments people make online. Even if such models were perfectly accurate, equipping ICE investigators with tools to search social media for ideas they consider threatening is ripe for abuse, particularly in an administration that conflates criticism with threats and regards viewpoints it dislikes as signs of terrorism . Moreover, Trump administration officials openly announced their intentions to use AI to monitor the internet for perceived support for Hamas among foreign students, which has often meant simply expressions of support for Palestinian rights, and ICE has sought to monitor social media for criticism of the agency . If this is the kind of AI usage the administration is willing to tell us about voluntarily, stronger transparency requirements would likely reveal considerably more. What Congress Should Do In the long term, Congress should pass several legislative reforms to rein in dangerous uses of AI. The Advancing American AI Act leaves it to each administration to decide what details agencies must disclose, which the current administration has interpreted narrowly to weaken the requirement. The Act should be amended to require federal agencies to disclose more meaningful detail in their inventories about how they are using AI. That must include reporting on the safeguards that agencies have put in place for any AI system that impacts people’s rights or safety. To limit ambiguity, the law should explicitly list certain applications of AI for which agencies must report safeguards, including AI systems used to inform decisions about whom to investigate, arrest, or deport. Agencies should also be required to update their inventories when a new use of AI is rolled out that has a significant impact – or would be presumed to have such an impact – on rights or safety. In the meantime, the House and Senate committees with jurisdiction over DHS ought to exercise their full oversight powers to bring this administration’s use of AI surveillance technologies out of the shadows, including compelling DHS officials to answer questions under oath. articles.title: FCC Leadership Pressures Broadcasters to Suppress Unfavorable Political Polling
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing “fake polls,” amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media. Carr’s post on X said, “Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis… Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations.” Carr urged broadcasters to “provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered.” In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very “context” that Carr said is needed. Carr’s post did not mention any specific fake polls or any specific broadcasters that aired them. The vagueness of Carr’s post may be useful for his and Trump’s ongoing battle against the news media. In August, Trump demanded that the FCC punish or rebuke an NBC journalist for saying he has “mixed results” in election endorsements, and wrote that the FCC must do something about “THE FAKE POLLS USED BY OUR CROOKED MEDIA.” Ex-FCC chairs: Carr wants “self-censorship” Carr’s latest warning to broadcasters came as no surprise, given that he has spent much of the past two years threatening broadcast licenses and opening investigations into Trump’s least favorite news companies. Former Republican and Democratic FCC chairs and commissioners recently said Carr is seeking to censor and chill the speech of broadcasters through a proceeding that threatens the licenses of ABC-owned stations . “FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s threat against broadcasters over their reporting on political polls is yet another truly outrageous attempt to censor and control the information available to Americans as they prepare to vote… Carr is now seizing on reports about fabricated political polling as an excuse to once again try to scare broadcasters into self-censorship,” said a statement today from a group of former FCC chairs and officials. Today’s statement was attributed to former Chairman Tom Wheeler, a Democrat; former Chairman Mark Fowler, a Republican; and seven former high-ranking FCC officials. “Good-faith reporting on public polls—even ones that turn out to be made up—is not a violation of the FCC’s news distortion or hoax rules. And the FCC has zero authority to dictate editorial decisions,” they said. Wheeler, Fowler, and others previously signed a letter objecting to the ABC investigation. The letter called it “the latest attack in a sustained campaign by Chairman Carr and the Trump administration of threatening legal sanctions against licensees whose speech President Trump dislikes.” Anna Gomez, the only Democratic commissioner on the current FCC, wrote today that “Pollsters who intentionally mislead the public should answer for it, but broadcasters who report publicly available polling data should never be punished when a poll is wrong. FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith.” Pollster admits hoax An entity called Wedgewood Polls said yesterday that it published fabricated polling data “to test whether media outlets, aggregators, and commentators would report on data without verifying the source, methodology, or underlying firm legitimacy.” It claimed to be running an experiment on the modern political polling industry. “Despite having no history, formal credentials, or real data behind the vast majority of our releases, Wedgewood Polling was added to major polling aggregators, including The New York Times, FiftyPlusOne, and VoteHub, and repeatedly treated as a legitimate news source,” the statement said. Notably, the three polling aggregators mentioned in the statement are not broadcast stations or news networks whose programming is carried on local broadcast stations. That’s relevant because Carr has repeatedly said he merely uses the FCC’s regulatory authority over broadcasters with licenses to use public spectrum, and not media outlets that do not have FCC licenses. Carr’s post yesterday warned broadcasters to “comply with their public interest obligations” under “the terms of their federal licenses.” While Wedgewood Polls claimed that its data faced no scrutiny from news organizations, FiftyPlusOne said it was preparing to publish an article exposing the fraud and had sent a request for comment to Wedgewood. “They did not respond to our request, but instead posted a public statement on social media admitting that they had been fabricating data,” FiftyPlusOne wrote . FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and VoteHub all say they did some vetting of Wedgewood before deciding to use its polls. FiftyPlusOne wrote: Their statement alleges that FiftyPlusOne, The New York Times, and other poll aggregators did not conduct appropriate vetting of their firm prior to aggregating their polls; this is false. We reached out to them to ask who they were and confirm the methodology statement on their website. We were given two names, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. We were able to independently confirm that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry and reviewed their methodology statement in detail. It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different. Wedgewood operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm, including collecting money from donors to conduct crowd-funded polls, and sharing raw survey data (which we now have confirmed was fraudulent) with FiftyPlusOne on Oct. 15, 2026. NYT and VoteHub explain poll inclusion VoteHub Head of Data Science Zachary Donnini said that after talking to Wedgewood’s “head pollster,” Votehub “assigned them a D grade and included their polling data on our site.” Meanwhile, the New York Times updated its polling page with a statement about Wedgewood. The New York Times said it sends all new pollsters “a series of questions regarding the identities of the pollsters; the methods they were using to draw their sample, contact respondents and weight their polls; and the source of their funding.” Wedgewood answered the questions, and the NYT used 15 of its polls for state and congressional-district races. The Wedgewood “polls were never included in the tracker or average of President Trump’s approval rating or of the national polls tracking overall preference for control of Congress,” the NYT said. In the previous incident this year, a group called Median Strategies admitted it faked poll results as part of a “social experiment.” The NYT said it never included that group’s results in its trackers “because the group did not respond to our questions about its methodology.” Nate Silver removed Wedgewood from his polling site today. Wedgewood polls tended to be about 1 percentage point more favorable for Democrats than other polls, according to Silver . Jon Brodkin Senior IT Reporter Jon Brodkin Senior IT Reporter 89 Comments

articles.title: SpaceX Readies Starship Mechanical Catch to Triple Launch Pace
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav In its current iteration, SpaceX is largely a data company seeking to provide enormous amounts of compute for artificial intelligence. During an earnings call on Tuesday afternoon, company officials spent much of their time discussing ambitious plans to roll out up to 10 GW of compute in 2027—on the ground. Gone are the days of aspirational talk about sending humans to Mars and settling the red planet. Now it is almost all about artificial intelligence and the data needed to support its expansion. However, the company’s long-term ambitions to provide data services from space, initially with the Starlink Internet constellation and eventually through the “Starmind” data center constellation, still rely on an actual rocket. That would be the Starship vehicle, and during the earnings call, SpaceX founder Elon Musk and the company’s president and chief operating officer, Gwynne Shotwell, provided new performance targets for the vehicle. It has been a little more than three weeks since the 14th test flight of the massive rocket, which largely went well despite some issues with the Raptor rocket engine. SpaceX has gleaned enough data from that test, Musk said, to attempt a catch of both the Super Heavy first stage of the rocket and the Starship upper stage on the next flight. Musk said he believes success is “more likely than not” for these attempts, but he added the company is hardware rich if there are failures. Both catches would happen at the company’s launch site in South Texas, Starbase. SpaceX is currently targeting November for this 15th test flight. Landing over land One of the big hurdles is regulatory, as the Starship vehicle must return to the launch site over land, including northern Mexico. “We have had significant constructive engagement with the FAA, and we expect the license for our Flight 15 to include return to launch site and tower catch for both stages,” Shotwell said. As for what comes after this test flight, Shotwell said SpaceX would attempt to refly a Starship upper stage “early” next year. The company will also seek to complete a long-delayed refueling test of Starship early in 2027. This Starship-to-Starship refueling demonstration is an important milestone for SpaceX and NASA to prove the viability of Starship being refueled in low-Earth orbit for lunar missions. Refueling on this scale has never been done before, and the company needs to get data on the efficiency of such transfers and the rate of boil-off of liquid oxygen and methane in space. This data will refine projections for how many launches are needed to support a Starship landing on the Moon for NASA as part of the Artemis Program. For SpaceX, the near-term priority is reaching a high flight cadence for Starship and pushing the boundaries of vehicle reuse to enable it. A weekly cadence? Musk, who often offers hyper-optimistic timeframes, said he expects Starship to reach a “weekly” flight cadence during the first half of 2027 and to launch twice weekly during the second half of the year. The key will be how much Starship can be reused. “The rate at which we launch Starship will increase dramatically as we solve rapid and complete reusability,” Musk said. “At first there will be a little bit of refurbishment that’s needed between each flight, and we’ll iron out the need for any refurbishment such that you can immediately land the rocket and launch it again, just like an airplane.” That’s the vision, at least. Achieving complete reusability with an orbital rocket has never been done before, so SpaceX’s engineering team will undoubtedly face some significant hurdles. Over time, however, they are likely to get close to the vision of launching, landing, and reflying rockets. SpaceX will largely focus on its own payloads in 2027 with the Starship rocket. Shotwell said the company would continue launching Starlink V3 satellites, the second generation of “mobile” satellites that deliver direct-to-cell connectivity, as well as Starmind data center prototypes, next year. During the earnings call, neither Musk nor Shotwell addressed, nor were asked by financial analysts, about the controversial throttling of Starlink capabilities for Ukraine in its war with Russia. articles.title: Southeast Asian AI Monetization Shifts Past Traditional SaaS Subscriptions
articles.content: LivestreamMenuSoutheast Asia's generative AI adoption has reached 243 million users in less than three years, according to Google, Temasek and Bain & Company.Only a small fraction of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, even as adoption accelerates.Businesses have generated AI commercial value through applications ranging from e-commerce to digital advertising, Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC.In this article Southeast Asia is embracing artificial intelligence at a rapid pace. But the business of making money from AI is about more than getting consumers to pay for it. Generative AI adoption in the region has reached around 243 million people in less than three years, according to the annual e-Conomy SEA report released Wednesday by Google, Temasek and Bain & Company. That is equivalent to 58% of the working population, with adoption occurring four times faster than the uptake of mobile internet. Yet only 1% to 2% of the region's population pays for personal AI subscriptions, highlighting a gap between widespread adoption and direct consumer spending. Florian Hoppe, a partner at Bain & Company, told CNBC in an interview that businesses have found other ways to generate AI's commercial value from online shopping to digital advertising. Companies have been using AI to improve e-commerce conversion rates and handle routine customer inquiries, allowing employees to focus on other tasks, he added. Consumers may also be paying indirectly for AI when purchasing products developed using the technology. The findings come as Southeast Asia's digital economy is projected to grow 17% to $368 billion in gross merchandise value this year, with the market expected to exceed $1 trillion by 2035, according to the report. Hoppe also pointed to another factor driving the region's enthusiasm for AI: its willingness to embrace new technologies as consumers have shown what he described as "pragmatic optimism" toward AI, embracing the technology for its practical benefits. The region has historically ranked among the most active users of major digital platforms on a per-capita basis. "They're very experimental," Hoppe said, describing consumers' openness to new tools and services. He also added that in terms of individual markets, Singapore is among Southeast Asia's early leaders in AI adoption. That openness is extending to more autonomous uses of AI, with 75% of users willing to let AI agents find the best prices and complete purchases on their behalf. The report shows that confidence is also growing, with 62% of respondents saying they trust AI tools more than they did a year ago. Despite the rapid adoption, people in Southeast Asia still use AI far less than those in the U.S., with usage per person at just 10% of U.S. levels. For businesses, however, the potential returns are becoming more tangible. About 69% of shoppers use AI to compare complex purchases such as electronics, while early case studies show AI helping businesses boost conversion rates by 10% year on year and increase the average amount customers spend per order by as much as 75%. An example is Shopee, a Southeast Asian e-commerce platform, which now handles approximately 80% of customer queries through AI chatbots, helping cut its cost per customer contact by 30% year on year. In online media, Hoppe pointed to a "significant uplift" in advertising click-through rates and conversions through AI-powered advertising and improved targeting. But the benefits extend beyond online shopping. AI is helping travelers plan trips, making digital advertising more effective and enabling voice-assisted bookings for ride-hailing and food delivery services. Southeast Asia's online travel market is projected to grow 10% to $59 billion in gross merchandise value this year. Online media revenue, including digital advertising and streaming, is expected to rise 22% to $44 billion, while ride-hailing and food delivery are forecast to grow 15% to $40 billion in gross merchandise value, according to the report.

articles.title: Karnataka Defers Youth Social Media Ban Decision to Indian Central Telecommunications Ministry
articles.content: Despite the Supreme Court’s recent order against a blanket social media ban and age-based restrictions, the Karnataka state government has said it will seek the Centre’s recommendations on restricting or banning social media access for children, according to a Deccan Herald report . Unnamed state officials reportedly said that a social media ban “comes under the Centre’s domain.” The state government has apparently realised that it can enforce restrictions only on devices under its control, not on all devices, such as those owned by parents. In this context, Karnataka’s Department of School Education & Literacy is likely to ask the state Cabinet to make recommendations next month, the report said.  “At the state-level, we will regulate the usage of computers in schools and colleges. A complete social media ban is a larger issue on which the Centre has to take a decision. This is a subject that comes under the Centre’s domain.” – Anonymous govt official.  What did the Supreme Court say about social media bans and restrictions? The Supreme Court’s October 15 order, which Karnataka’s Additional Chief Secretary of School Education & Literacy, Rashmi V Mahesh, referred to, also discussed age-based restrictions on social media. As MediaNama reported , the bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and K.V. Chandran made the following two points about social media bans and restrictions: “…we have no hesitation in saying that the right to access and use the internet is a fundamental right of every individual under Article 21 read with Article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution. Our children, irrespective of their age, enjoy the same rights, and to deny the same altogether would be as absurd as saying children below a certain age do not have a conscience worth protecting or a freedom of speech worth expressing. The safety of our children and their freedom are not at odds with each other. Our children are entitled to both. The means by which measures relating to age-based restrictions are achieved are themselves an overreach. Such processes, inevitably, always require identifying and ascertaining the age of each and every user, continuous collection and monitoring of sensitive data and an overall disproportionate risk of misuse and surveillance, the kind which finds no place within the right to privacy of our people.” –  Supreme Court. How the Karnataka government is approaching a social media ban : In the 2026–27 Budget, then Chief Minister Siddaramaiah had said: “With the objective of preventing adverse effects of increasing mobile usage on children, usage of social media will be banned for children under the age of 16.” – Then Karnataka CM. At the time of the announcement, as MediaNama reported , neither the government nor any member of the Legislative Assembly (MLA) had introduced or presented a draft Bill on the proposed social media ban in the Assembly. While the then Chief Minister had spoken of a ban, Information Technology Minister Priyank Kharge told Deccan Herald that the government was still in discussions with social media platforms and was possibly exploring algorithm-based regulations. “We’re trying to see how we can regulate [access]…In Australia and other countries that banned social media, we’ve seen children bypassing the age verification step. So, now, we’re trying to see how algorithms can be regulated.” – Karnataka IT Minister Priyank Kharge Additional Chief Secretary of School Education & Literacy Rashmi V Mahesh referred to the Supreme Court’s October 15 order without specifically discussing the proposed ban or restrictions. She said the Supreme Court’s judgment “aligns well with the state government’s interventions,” such as the inclusion of computers and artificial intelligence (AI) in its teaching methods. The age-based approach being considered by the Centre : Days after Karnataka’s announcement, government sources said the Centre was preparing a three-tier framework for children aged 8–12, 12–16, and 16–18, instead of imposing a blanket ban. On August 20, the Delhi High Court declined to order a ban , leaving the matter to the government. In September, Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the Supreme Court that the Centre would amend the Information Technology Rules to prevent platforms from allowing users under 18 to create accounts. What makes a state-level social media ban difficult to implement ? In an article , MediaNama founder and editor Nikhil Pahwa highlighted the difficulties of implementing a social media ban at the state level. “The difference between ten years ago and now is that companies do have geolocation data based on IP addresses. But geolocation is largely inaccurate. Sometimes you log in to Gmail in Delhi, and the login confirmation that hits your phone, assumes you’re in Noida or Ghaziabad. In instances where state boundaries are very close, like Karnataka and Tamil Nadu, you’re going to create a geolocation conflict. I f one state bans and the other doesn’t, how exactly are platforms supposed to enforce that? Unfortunately, the way regulators think about this is, ‘Our job is to impose a restriction, your job is to implement it, so it’s your problem.’ But it doesn’t work like that, because you’re effectively asking for something that may not be technically feasible. Feasibility should also be taken into consideration when creating law. “ – Nilhil Pahwa Pahwa also attributed state-level action to the Union Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology’s (MeitY) inaction. “There is a trend of states bringing out laws specific to the Internet, and this fragmentation of laws governing the Internet is problematic and because the Internet transcends physical boundaries, and it’s better if the Centre does it…. So States are trying to fill the gap left by MEITY’s abdication of responsibility. The inaction from the Centre nudges the states to act. Expect more state action on Social Media, not less,” he wrote. Could regulating social media algorithms and design offer an alternative? Kharge’s remark that the state government is now examining how algorithms can be regulated raises a question Pahwa posed in February. “The problem is that instead of regulating the system, governments are regulating access to the system,” Pahwa argued in his criticism of blanket social media bans. However, neither the Centre nor the state government currently has a framework or policy for regulating social media algorithms to mitigate the risks and harms these platforms pose to children. “The conversation should move from safety by design to safety by defaul t. All your opt-in options that aren’t privacy-centric should be checked off by default , such as location sharing and content access for under 18s. Safety by design is a good philosophy for a new platform, but it’s time to move to safety by default,” – a speaker at the Medianama event.   Explore MediaNama’s coverage of what experts said about whether changes to social media design could offer an alternative to blanket bans or restrictions. articles.title: US Capital Concentration Reaches Historic Peak on Delayed AI Returns
articles.content: Americans have placed an unprecedented bet on the transformative power of artificial intelligence. The past 50 years of economic history suggests it won’t pay off, at least not on a timetable the market expects. Not since the Gilded Age—when, in 1885, railroad stocks accounted for more than 80% of active trading on the New York Stock Exchange—has the U.S. economy wagered so much on a single theme. When that bubble burst in the Panic of 1893, a third of railroads went bust, more than 500 banks failed, and the economy plunged into a four-year depression. Today’s frantic AI buildout may be on a similar trajectory. AI-related capital spending has surged to about 2% of U.S. GDP , from near zero five years ago. But this time, the AI wager is concentrated in far fewer companies than the railway mania ever was. In January, the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis reported that investments in information processing equipment, software, research and development, and data centers—four investment categories economists consider the closest proxies for AI investment—accounted for 39% of U.S. economic growth in the first three quarters of 2025, higher than the 28% those activities contributed in 2000, the peak of the dot-com boom. Pantheon Macroeconomics calculates that without AI spending, U.S. corporate investment in equipment was negative last year. Consumption, too, is heavily dependent on AI. The top 20% of income earners now account for approximately 60% of all U.S. consumer spending , according to Moody’s Analytics. The source of their wealth? The AI stock rally. AI has become the dominant theme across all segments of U.S. capital markets. In equities, the “Magnificent Seven”— Alphabet , Amazon , Apple , Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Tesla—boast a combined $25 trillion in market capitalization. That’s 35% of the value of the S&P 500 and the highest concentration in a handful of stocks since just before the crash of 1929. Separately, research from the Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City shows that AI-related companies’ share of investment-grade bond issuance increased from 2% in 2023 to 10% in 2026 , highlighting the growing concentration of this kind of borrowing in credit markets. In venture capital, AI captured 81% of a record $300 billion in global venture funding in the first quarter of 2026, and just four companies—OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, and Waymo—absorbed two-thirds of the total. The result is a self-reinforcing loop. Hyperscalers will spend $800 billion this year on chips, data centers, and the power to run them, propping up GDP growth. Investors are bidding up AI stocks, fattening the portfolios of the richest 20%, whose spending boosts consumption. As the buildout outgrows hyperscalers’ cash flow, new investment is increasingly financed by debt and off-balance-sheet partnerships. The U.S. growth engine now runs on a narrow set of mutually reinforcing drivers. If one stalls, the others lose power too. The Bank for International Settlements warns in its 2026 Annual Economic Report that AI exuberance risks ending in a “lengthy investment bust.” The BIS flagged “circular financing” as a core vulnerability, more than half of investment in AI firms comes from other AI firms, with recipients using that money to buy their backers’ products. Profits are being funded by investors rather than end customers. America’s AI bet is underwritten by a single assumption: That by 2027, growth driven by infrastructure will hand off to growth driven by AI-powered efficiency gains across the broader economy. I think that’ll come much later than the market expects. As I argued in Fortune a few weeks ago, five decades of digital innovation achieved broad consumer adoption yet came with a decline in aggregate productivity growth. This is the Innovation Paradox: more innovation and slower growth. Technology diffusion follows a double K-shaped pattern. Consumers adopt almost immediately; enterprises, at a glacial pace. Within enterprises, a handful of superstar firms embrace new technologies quickly while the rest struggle to make use of them. The structure of the U.S. economy makes things even worse. The U.S. has shifted from vertically-linked industrial sectors—where innovations could naturally travel through supply chains—to horizontally spread service sectors that resist transformation because they depend on human judgment. These “stagnant” sectors, as the economist William Baumol called them, now account for roughly half of GDP in advanced economies. Firms are also saddled with debilitating administrative and regulatory compliance costs, which I estimate are now past the topping point at which they strangle innovation. Adding to the paradox: the concentration of capital in AI-linked companies starves the rest of the economy of investment needed to be AI-ready. If hospitals, schools, logistics companies, and retailers can’t invest in digital infrastructure and workforce retraining, the broad-based productivity gains that justify today’s AI valuations will never arrive. AI could still defy the paradox: unlike previous digital waves, it is a cognitive technology that can reason and make judgments, precisely what’s needed to unlock productivity in labor-intensive Baumol sectors. But only deep adoption across a broad spectrum of the economy will realize that potential. Firms need to allocate capital to workers and workflows, not just chips and data centers. That’s a possible silver lining if the AI bubble bursts—that the assets financed by irrationally exuberant investors end up reshaping the economy for the better. Canals in the 1830s, railroads in the 1880s, electrification in the 1920s, telecoms and the internet in the late 1990s—each ended in painful collapse, yet the physical infrastructure created in those speculative booms laid the foundations for decades of later prosperity. Will data centers, semiconductors, and AI models prove equally long-lasting? Perhaps. But that process will take decades, not months or years. In the short term, the more concentrated the bet, the more severe the potential reckoning. No prior bubble spanned so many dimensions of the economy simultaneously—GDP growth, consumer spending, equity markets, debt markets, and venture capital all tethered to a single theme. That is not an economic launchpad. It is a vulnerability of historic proportions. articles.title: Civil Liberties Groups Challenge Big Tech Interoperability Security Excuses
articles.content: An open internet where people can freely build, share, and remix each other's work is a powerful engine of grassroots innovation we’ve all benefited from. In recent decades, however, corporations have taken control of an increasing share of this work, giving them a greater ability to stifle challengers and limit our choices. When regulators address this by mandating that tech giants play fair by requiring interoperability, the gatekeepers respond with a tired refrain: Playing fair puts users’ security at risk. Unfortunately for these trillion-dollar companies, this gotcha isn’t the end of the conversation. Regulators can ensure that meaningful choice and security thrive. Lawmakers have been catching up, recognizing that the best way to rein in big tech is to require these oligopolies to open up their platforms to independent developers. As we explained six years ago , mandating interoperability helps prevent the misuse of people’s data and enables more privacy-respecting alternatives. Tech giants, in contrast, have been arguing that our data is safer when they have exclusive control. Tech Giants Claim Interoperability Means Insecurity The European Union’s Digital Markets Act (DMA) put interoperability into law under Article 6(7): “gatekeeper shall allow providers of services and providers of hardware, free of charge, effective interoperability with” a designated Core Platform Service they operate. The language describes an unambiguous requirement to remediate vendor lockouts and anti-competitive behavior of the major service operators—it is not optional. Apple claimed that enforcing this obligation in mobile app stores would put their customers at risk and do irreparable harm to trust in their brand. It’s an argument reminiscent of Apple’s fight against the right to repair , and in both instances the company is fighting to maintain its restrictive ecosystem to stop people from finding better deals elsewhere. Apple has long cultivated a more corporate-controlled experience with the iPhone, but this argument is now also being used for the relatively-more-open Android devices from Google. In the same year Apple argued against the DMA, Epic Games sued Google for its restrictive terms of service and extractive policies for revenue generated in apps. Google predictably alleged that opening up its platform to other app stores it couldn’t vet would allow harmful apps to be installed. The case was ultimately decided this year in the U.S. federal appeals court for the Ninth Circuit, with the court rejecting this argument, dealing a blow to Google’s feudal security arrangement, and paving the way for third-party app stores to be delivered as apps via the Google Play Store . Interoperating Secure Systems Can (and Should) Exist Policymakers cannot take tech giants’ claims at face value. Companies have every incentive to resist interoperability requirements, because interoperability lowers practical barriers and reduces switching costs for consumers adopting competing services. Even where companies offer credible claims from internal technical and security experts, independent experts rarely have the access and information they need to test those claims. Companies have selectively made arguments that security is harmed by interoperability, often in contexts which are to their advantage. These companies are happy to let a general misconception flourish which frames security as inherently opposed to interoperability. This narrative is wrong. We’ve seen that when interoperability and information security are both set as essential and non-negotiable criteria, secure interoperable systems result—systems that don’t sacrifice the rich features we’ve come to expect of the services we rely on. The cross-platform rollout of Rich Communication Services (RCS), and now Message Layer Security (MLS) on top of it is a perfect example of this, creating end-to-end secure messaging by default between Android and iOS. For RCS and MLS, Google was conveniently on the other side of the interoperability argument, campaigning Apple to adopt the standard to overcome the diminished “green bubble” experience iPhone users had when texting non-iPhone users. Once Apple finally agreed to interoperate by implementing common standards, all users benefited from improved messaging security. In cases where legitimate security concerns are raised, these can be assessed and remedied on a case-by-case basis, without sacrificing user agency. Striking the Right Balance Retrofitting interoperability into already secure closed systems shouldn’t be done carelessly: it requires regulators strike the right balance of pressure and leniency to allow the time and precision necessary to make these renovations. Any components developed with the assumption of privileged access by trusted parties (e.g. your browser engine ) are particularly vulnerable to serious security risks when opened up to unaccountable third parties. By adapting interoperability and information security as essential design principles, we can expect more safety, but also more freedom. With regard to the DMA, when security concerns are legitimate, we urge the European Commission to work with companies and outside experts to offer guidance in technical implementation and provide clarity on regulatory compliance. This approach paves a path forward that balances the interest of legal oversight and the needs of the companies alike. Policymakers wishing to uproot these unfair platforms of control must do so with care and limit the impact this disruption can have. But security concerns must not act as a lever to indefinitely delay compliance. Closed systems should be impartially evaluated, and if concerns are valid, regulators can allow more time and guidance to be given to companies implementing these changes. One possibility is a tiered approach: offering leniency during an initial period where systems need to be retrofitted to abide by new requirements, followed by a subsequent and ongoing stricter observance of fair play. Once interoperability and information security are adopted as essential design principles, further development with these rights-enhancing principles in mind will more easily follow. The result will be an internet the world deserves—where we can expect more safety, but also more freedom.

articles.title: CashApp Identity Theft Leads to Wrongful Criminal Incarceration
articles.content: • Someone Opened a CashApp In Her Name. She Faces Years in Prison · Oct 21, 2026 at 9:59 AM Amanda Smith is charged with computer fraud due to a scam CashApp account being in her name. But in a Kafkaesque situation, CashApp won't provide her any information because she can't prove she is the owner. Amanda Smith answered the door one afternoon in April and came face to face with the local Sheriff’s department in upstate Pennsylvania. The officers said they had a warrant for her arrest for a crime she had allegedly committed more than a thousand miles away in Arkansas. “I was completely confused,” Smith recalled. For one, she had never been to Arkansas. Second, the warrant was for computer fraud. By her own admission, Smith was not a very tech savvy person. She had a feeling she was being set up. After discussing with the officers the practicalities of what was about to happen — she was allowed to get her contact lenses — they took her away in handcuffs to the local jail where she spent three nights. The reason for Smith’s arrest, she learned later, was that a scammer had tricked someone on Facebook Marketplace into sending $1,000 to a CashApp account in her name that the scammer controlled. The scammer created the account using her Social Security number and date of birth. Smith said she has never used CashApp. What developed over the next few days, and has now stretched across six months, is a Kafkaesque situation in which Smith, in her telling, is being asked to prove her innocence in an ongoing criminal case, while CashApp refuses to provide her any information about the account because she couldn’t prove that she was the owner. The case shows the very real danger of identity theft, how the data and tools offered to police can lead them to the wrong person, and the sprawling world of CashApp fraud, where scammers and money launderers create or compromise accounts to make and move money quickly. Along the way, ordinary people may not just lose money, but their freedom too. Smith faces up to six years in prison for the charges. “They're trying to turn it into my problem [...] that I need to prove that I'm innocent,” Smith told 404 Media. “That's not what I grew up believing was the way it worked.” Image: Amanda Smith, courtesy of Smith. According to a copy of the prosecuting attorney’s affidavit form, police responded to an Arkansas address on February 4 after a report of fraud. The victim said they recently found some items for sale on Facebook Marketplace. When the victim messaged about buying the items, the seller told him to send money to his wife’s CashApp account, which he did. That account was in the name Amanda Smith and had the username $Smithy5687. It turned out, the seller’s Facebook account was hacked. The seller wasn’t really selling the items at all, and the person had been scammed. The CashApp account was created just shortly before the scam, at the end of January. Investigators then took the CashApp account’s username and served Block Inc., which owns CashApp, with a search warrant seeking information connected to the account. The data CashApp returned included Smith’s SSN and date of birth (CashApp requires users to provide their SSN to, ironically, protect against fraud). That led investigators to the Amanda Smith, 47, who they later arrested.  Detective Poole said he then further confirmed the information on the account by obtaining a copy of Smith’s drivers’ license and “by also running her information through Accurint.” Accurint is a tool made by LexisNexis that cops use to query public and proprietary records. “Det [Detective] Poole sent a search warrant to Cash App. The information received from Cash App showed the account receiving the $1000 belonged to D [defendant, Amanda Smith],” the case record reads. Smith is charged with computer fraud, unlawful use of a communication device, and theft of property, according to a court filing. “I was basically in shock,” Smith said of her three nights in the local jail. She was sleep deprived, with the lights constantly on and a guard flashing a light in her cell every hour. During that time, Smith did not actually know why she was arrested, she said. Days later she was chained and shackled and taken into court for her extradition hearing.  Her bail was set at $50,000, but Smith recalled authorities told her not to bother paying it because they intended to keep her detained to extradite to Arkansas anyway. She was released and had to make her own way to Arkansas the following week for a court appearance. Smith and her husband Josh drove, not wanting to rely on a flight’s schedule to get there, Smith said. She was nervous authorities might arrest her once again. After the hearing, authorities took Smith’s fingerprints and mugshot. After another $20,000 bail, she was free to return to Pennsylvania, but now awaits the outcome of the case. If found guilty, she could spend years in prison.  💡 Do you know anything else about CashApp fraud or similar cases to this one? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co. The CashApp account was made with Smith’s SSN and date of birth, but a lot of other information from the account does not line up with Smith, according to 404 Media’s review of the data produced during discovery. The Philadelphia address on it is not Smith’s or Josh’s, nor one either of them have ever lived in. They said they lived together in Philadelphia in the same ZIP code as the address on the CashApp account, but not that address, and they don’t live in Philadelphia anymore. Smith said the phone number used to create the CashApp account is not her current number. Her husband did not remember Smith using that phone number at all, although Smith said she may have done so in the early 2000s before she switched from T-Mobile to AT&T. 404 Media did find this phone number linked to an Amanda Smith in various data breaches from years ago using data from cybersecurity company District 4 Labs . Using data from open source intelligence company OSINT Industries , 404 Media found someone made a Venmo account using the same phone number but under another name entirely. Whoever made that account did so around a week before the scam CashApp account. The CashApp data also shows whoever made the account used an iPhone running 16.1.1, a very out of date operating system from 2022. Smith, however, has an iPhone 13 mini with iOS 26.5.2, according to a screenshot of her device’s settings she shared with 404 Media.  The IP addresses used during the creation of the CashApp account, and during the scam itself, relate to connections from Verizon’s wireless network, 404 Media found by querying IP geolocation tools. Again, Smith is on an AT&T plan, and says she has never had a Verizon plan. Smith said she has never used the username “smithy5687.” 404 Media found other people online using this moniker, but none appeared to be Smith. A screenshot of a court record in Smith's case. Smith’s leading theory is that someone stole her identity, perhaps through a data breach like the National Public Data breach in December 2024 , and used that information to open the CashApp account. Smith only received this CashApp data through discovery in her case. When she contacted CashApp herself initially, “CashApp refused to provide me with any information about the account, because I couldn't prove that I was the owner ,” she told 404 Media. Smith hired a private investigator to review the case and data provided by CashApp. “I have been investigating the circumstances surrounding Amanda Smith’s case, and I believe there are legitimate questions about the evidence used to identify her as the person responsible for the alleged activity,” Max Ponte, the investigator, told 404 Media in an email. “The central issue is the distinction between identifying a person by name and establishing that the person actually operated or controlled an account. Based on my review of the available case materials, I have concerns about whether investigators sufficiently established that connection before pursuing criminal charges against Amanda.” “I am actively trying to get Amanda's case dismissed short of a jury trial,” Jason Horton, Smith’s lawyer, told 404 Media in an email. “Amanda, Josh, and Mr. Ponte have provided significant information that supports Amanda's position that her charges should [be] dismissed, or, at the very least, should have been further investigated prior to Amanda's arrest. Although I do not comment on the specifics of pending cases, I will say I will do all I can to make sure justice is served in this case.” CashApp did not respond to multiple requests for comment about the case and its verification procedures. Jeffrey Sams, the prosecutor in the case, did not respond to a request for comment asking if investigators took any additional steps to verify the CashApp data specifically beyond what was mentioned in the detective’s telling in court records. CashApp is a common vehicle for scammers, fraudsters, and hackers. I’ve previously reported how hackers were breaking into and emptying CashApp accounts, with CashApp sometimes refusing to reimburse the stolen funds. On Telegram, many criminals offer CashApp related services, such as cashing out accounts. In Smith’s case, it appears CashApp was the method not just to get $1,000 from a target, but also then to distribute the funds. Once the scam account received the $1,000, it sent small chunks of the money to a web of other accounts just hours later, according to the CashApp data. Some of those also appear to be scammer controlled; some of their usernames have changed from one name to a different one entirely. Authorities have offered Smith a plea deal of a $1,000 fine, $1,000 restitution, various other costs like a bailiff and DNA sample fee, and three years probation. Smith said she refuses to accept it because she is innocent, and doing so would have long term negative consequences on her life. “I was basically thinking, oh well, it’ll get dismissed,” Smith told 404 Media. That didn’t happen, and the case is progressing, with Smith feeling constantly anxious. A hearing is now scheduled for November. Smith said, “I am just waiting and seeing.” Joseph is an award-winning investigative journalist focused on generating impact. His work has triggered hundreds of millions of dollars worth of fines, shut down tech companies, and much more. More from Joseph Cox • •

articles.title: European Origin Rules on Electric Vehicles Spark Industrial Shifts
articles.content: Stellen große Unternehmen ihre Flotten schneller auf Elektroautos aus europäischer Fertigung um, könnten in Deutschland bis 2030 bis zu 134.000 zusätzliche Vollzeitstellen entstehen. Das ist das Ergebnis einer Modellrechnung des Fraunhofer-Instituts für System- und Innovationsforschung (ISI), die der Verkehrs- und Umweltverband Transport & Environment (T&E) in Auftrag gegeben hat. Sie bezieht sich auf die geplante EU-Verordnung Clean Corporate Vehicles Regulation (CCVR) zu emissionsarmen Firmenautos. Laut T&E Deutschland kämen in diesem Szenario zwischen 2026 und 2030 rund 7,8 Milliarden Euro zusätzliche Wertschöpfung und bis zu 4,7 Milliarden Euro an Investitionen hinzu. Auf Deutschland entfielen etwa 39 Prozent der EU-weit berechneten 344.000 zusätzlichen Stellen. Mit deutlichem Abstand folgen Polen mit 38.500 und die Slowakei mit 26.200 Jobs. Die Verteilung ergibt sich aus der bereits vorhandenen Fahrzeug- und Batterieproduktion in den jeweiligen Ländern. Das Ergebnis beruht auf einer Modellannahme, Zusagen einzelner Hersteller gibt es dazu noch nicht. Verglichen wurden drei Varianten für das Jahr 2030. Im Basisszenario, das allein den CO₂-Flottengrenzwerten für Pkw folgt, ist der Firmenwagenmarkt zu 47 Prozent elektrifiziert. Im moderaten Szenario greifen CCVR und Made-in-Europe-Vorgaben, die finanziellen Anreize aus Artikel 4 des Entwurfs wirken aber nur verhalten. Mit diesen Annahmen steigt der Anteil auf 52 Prozent. Erst im starken Szenario, in dem Förderung und Steuervorteile Verbrenner deutlich schneller aus den Flotten drängen, erreicht er 69 Prozent. EU-weit liegen die Effekte entsprechend weit auseinander: 196.000 zusätzliche Stellen im moderaten, 344.000 im starken Fall. Die Zahl von 134.000 Stellen für Deutschland entstammt dem starken Szenario. Gezählt werden Vollzeitäquivalente, die das Modell aus den Arbeitskosten der angenommenen europäischen Mehrproduktion ableitet. Sie umfassen Stellen in der Fahrzeug- und Komponentenfertigung, bei Zulieferern sowie induzierte Beschäftigung, die durch die Ausgaben der Beschäftigten entsteht. „Zusätzlich“ heißt dabei: mehr als im Basisszenario. Eine vollständige Gegenrechnung wegfallender Arbeitsplätze in der Verbrennerfertigung und bei klassischen Zulieferern geht aus der veröffentlichten Methodik nicht hervor. Als gesicherter Nettozuwachs der deutschen Gesamtbeschäftigung taugen die 134.000 also nicht, zumal der Auftraggeber selbst für schärfere Regeln wirbt. Besonders ausführlich betrachtet die Studie den Volkswagenkonzern, der im Firmenwagengeschäft und bei elektrischen Dienstwagen stark vertreten ist. Im moderaten Szenario würde Volkswagen bis 2030 rund 99.000 zusätzliche Elektroautos an europäische Firmenkunden verkaufen, im starken rund 590.000. T&E setzt das ins Verhältnis zur eigenen Annahme eines Abbaus der Produktionskapazität bei Volkswagen um 700.000 Fahrzeuge: Die Mehrverkäufe entsprächen 14 beziehungsweise 84 Prozent dieser Menge. Daraus leitet das Modell 14.000 beziehungsweise 56.300 direkte Vollzeitstellen ab. Auf die vier deutschen Werke Emden, Zwickau, Hannover und Neckarsulm, für die der Konzern laut seinem „Future Plan 2030“ ab 2031 keine wettbewerbsfähige Folgebelegung garantieren kann, entfielen 6300 beziehungsweise 25.400 Stellen. Für das moderate Szenario veranschlagt T&E dafür Investitionen von rund 760 Millionen Euro. Auch diese Werte sind eine rechnerische Zuordnung und keine geplanten Produktionszahlen. Ob Volkswagen zusätzliche Fahrzeuge tatsächlich dort baut, sagt die Studie nicht. Offen bleibt zudem der Beitrag der Batteriezellen: Würden alle zusätzlichen Autos mit Zellen der Konzerntochter PowerCo ausgestattet, fiele der Beschäftigungseffekt laut T&E noch höher aus. Eine Zahl dazu nennt der Verband aber nicht. Die EU-Kommission hat den Vorschlag für die CCVR am 16. Dezember 2025 vorgelegt. Er betrifft Neuzulassungen von Pkw und leichten Nutzfahrzeugen durch große Unternehmen im Sinne der EU-Bilanzrichtlinie, die zwei von drei Schwellen überschreiten: 250 Beschäftigte, 50 Millionen Euro Umsatz oder 25 Millionen Euro Bilanzsumme. Kleine und mittlere Betriebe sowie Privatleute bleiben außen vor. EU-weit sollen 2030 mindestens 45 Prozent der neu zugelassenen Firmen-Pkw lokal emissionsfrei sein, für Deutschland sieht der Entwurf sogar 54 Prozent vor, bei 83 Prozent lokal emissionsfreien oder -armen Fahrzeugen. Die Ziele gelten für die jährlichen Zulassungen, nicht für den Bestand, und sie verpflichten die Mitgliedstaaten, nicht einzelne Unternehmen. Über die Förderung entscheidet die Herkunft: Ab 1. Januar 2028 sollen staatliche Vergünstigungen für Firmenwagen nur noch für lokal emissionsfreie oder -arme Modelle fließen, die als „made in the European Union“ gelten. Welcher Anteil von Batterie, Antrieb oder Elektronik dafür aus Europa stammen muss, will die Kommission erst später per delegiertem Rechtsakt festlegen. T&E rechnet mit einer weiten Definition, die neben der EU auch die EFTA-Staaten und Großbritannien einschließt. Importierte Autos dürften Firmen natürlich weiterhin zulassen, nur eben ohne Förderung. Ob das die Produktion in Europa steigern kann, hängt von Modellangebot, Kapazitäten und Investitionsentscheidungen ab. Die CCVR ist nicht der einzige mögliche Faktor für einen Beschäftigungszuwachs. Ähnlich könnten sich strengere Made-in-EU-Vorgaben für die Autoproduktion im Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) auswirken. Dieses Gesetz soll festlegen, wann Autos als europäisch gelten und deshalb bei öffentlichen Aufträgen oder Förderprogrammen bevorzugt werden können. Bundeskanzler Friedrich Merz (CDU) und Frankreichs Präsident Emmanuel Macron hatten sich auf ein Tauschgeschäft verständigt: Deutschland akzeptiert eine schärfere Definition und härtere Regeln für Autos „Made in EU“, Frankreich unterstützt dafür eine Aufweichung des sogenannten „Verbrenner-Endes“ .
