articles.title: Century-Old Chestnut Groves Threatened by Data Center Infrastructure Expansion
articles.content: • The Chestnut Grove Caught in the Middle of A Years-Long Data Center Fight · Oct 21, 2026 at 9:31 AM A small grove of historic American chestnut trees has become the site of resistance against an AI data center in West Virginia. Near the bank of the Ohio River, a historic American chestnut grove in Mason County, West Virginia has become the epicenter of a fight against a planned 2,250 acre data center campus. Plans for the UK-based startup Nscale’s Monarch Compute Campus, with clients including Anthropic , Nvidia and Microsoft , encompass the former Clements State Nursery and the American chestnut trees still growing there.  For thousands of years, the American chestnut tree was a staple of life. Its natural range spanned hundreds of millions of acres from Maine to Mississippi , centuries before those names existed. As many as four billion trees provided a hearty nut crop for humans and provided miraculously rot-resistant lumber for railroad ties and housing. It sustained black bears as they prepared to hibernate, fed white-tailed deer and turkey, and shed nutrient-dense leaves. The largest American chestnut trees once grew 100 feet tall and 13 feet wide and represented one-fourth of all hardwoods ; a squirrel could scamper along their branches from New England to Georgia without touching the ground, as an old saying goes .  In 1904, a forester at the Bronx zoo noticed something alarming among their American chestnuts: The trees were dying en masse , struck by a mysterious blight. Within 40 years , that blight — thought to be brought to America on Asian chestnut trees — wiped out the tree’s population to near-extinction. Since then, conservationists have worked to restore American Chestnut trees and breed blight-resistant specimens. Typically, threats to groves include pests, climate change, and the fungus that destroyed their ancestors. Today, however, a new threat has entered the picture: data centers.  Library of Congress: American Chestnut Tree, Negative No. 6032 (Photographer and date unknown). "THIS GHOST FOREST OF BLIGHTED CHESTNUTS ONCE STOOD APPROXIMATELY AT THE LOCATION OF THE BYRD VISITOR CENTER." - Skyline Drive, From Front Royal, VA to Rockfish Gap, VA, Luray, Page County, VA Across the country, communities are pushing back against massive hyperscale data center projects, protesting against the noise pollution , environmental impacts , and blow to property values near these computer warehouses. In many places, elected officials are forging ahead to allow these multi-billion dollar deals in direct defiance of their constituents' wishes. Earlier this year, an Oklahoma farmer was arrested at a town hall meeting for speaking over his time against a 255-acre data center . Data centers are easy to build but much harder and slower to power, and their workarounds are egregious; For example, Elon Musk’s xAI Colossus 2 data center in Tennessee skips the local grid and runs its own natural gas turbines, worsening pollution and disproportionately impacting Black neighborhoods . But this tiny plot of American chestnut trees, just a little over an acre of land, has become a site of resistance in West Virginia.  A Small Town Is Fighting a $1.2 Billion AI Datacenter for America's Nuclear Weapon Scientists Ypsilanti, Michigan has officially decided to fight against the construction of a 'high-performance computing facility' that would service a nuclear weapons laboratory 1,500 miles away. Matthew Gault I first heard about the Clements chestnut grove after a 404 Media reader emailed me about it earlier this month, saying that the trees faced “potential destruction after November 1, 2026.” Social media posts called the threat “ urgent ,” and claimed bulldozers are lined up, with headlines declaring the grove is “ about to be destroyed .” In the last few weeks, the plight of a grove of fragile chestnut trees trembling in the shadow of a data center has gone viral. Goldberry Grove, a local regenerative chestnut orchard, posted “They’re bulldozing the American chestnuts after November 1st,” sparking more outrage.  In 2023, Governor Jim Justice announced a multi-billion dollar deal with Fidelis New Energy for a lifecycle carbon neutral hydrogen production facility, including the “Mountaineer GigaSystem” and the Monarch Compute Campus . Nscale acquired the American Intelligence & Power Corporation, sponsored by Fidelis New Energy and including the Monarch campus, in March.  “The citizens of Mason County are elated with the announcement of Fidelis New Energy selecting Mason County, West Virginia, for its multibillion-dollar state of the art carbon neutral, clean hydrogen complex,” John Musgrave, the Executive Director of the Mason County Development Authority said in Justice’s 2023 press release about the new data center plans.  With construction of the campus underway today, citizens do not seem elated. In September, heavy storms reportedly caused neighborhoods nearby to flood, as runoff from the construction site sent water and debris into adjacent properties as a section of the site’s fencing gave out. The Department of Environmental Protections (DEP) ordered Nscale “to immediately repair and strengthen the stormwater controls that failed, install additional erosion and sediment controls where needed, and take whatever actions are necessary to prevent similar releases from occurring in the future.” Nscale told local news outlet WOWK 13 that it would pay for the damage. Separately, the company is trying to buy out homeowners, but the people living there are resistant. “What they’re saying is one thing, but they’ve got to prove it,” one homeowner told WOWK 13 . “I’m staying. Fight for every one of these people.”  The fate of the trees has been a conversation among conservationists in the area for years. The American Chestnut Foundation (TACF) raised the issue in its May 2024 monthly newsletter : “Several communications have been made with [West Virginia Secretary of Commerce James Bailey] and he is aware of the chestnut trees at Clements. He assured the WV chapter that the trees will remain and be taken care of by Fidelis.”  The newsletter bulletin continued: “Mr. Bailey stated, ‘We value the chestnuts and will ensure that they are cared for. The state maintains ownership and control of the property, but if that ever changes, then the trees will be taken care of.’” The TACF noted that the future of the grove was “unclear.” Three years later, the picture is sharpening, as chestnut experts and the data center developers clash.  Sixty-two years ago, the first seedlings shipped out from West Virginia’s newly-designated Clements State Tree Nursery. The nursery was once owned by Mark Twain’s grandparents. The West Virginia Division of Natural Resources bought it in 1961 and the Division of Forestry operated it for decades onward. The nursery sold seedlings of several varieties of trees and kept 15 to 20 chestnut trees that showed promising traits of blight resistance. In 2021, the Charleston Gazette-Mail reported that the DNR quietly ceased operating the nursery, citing funding issues. “It was never set up to make money, but it was also never set up to lose the kind of money it’s been losing in the past 10 years,” then-Division of Forestry Director Tom Cover told the Gazette-Mail at the time.  "The Dying Chestnut Tree, My Teacher" (1927) and "The Dying Chestnut" (1919), by Alfred Stieglitz. Today, all of the American chestnut trees remaining at the former nursery site are infected with the blight fungus, Mark Double, a past president of the West Virginia Chapter of TACF told me. Many have died over the years, he said, but most of the trees still have sufficient resistance to have survived for 35 years, in spite of multiple infections. “The WV chapter of The American Chestnut Foundation has been harvesting nuts from this orchard for more than a decade,” Double told me over email.  Nscale’s Monarch campus is one of two data center projects planned for the area. Project Tamarack, which is owned by Starwood Digital Ventures, is planned for 10 miles south of the Monarch campus. West Virginia Governor Patrick Morrisey announced the project early last month. Morrisey promises 1,000 temporary jobs but just 300 permanent positions as a result of the project. Research shows that data centers rarely live up to promises about bolstering local economies. “Data centers do not bring high-paying tech jobs to local communities because they operate as infrastructure projects rather than traditional jobcreating businesses,” University of Michigan researchers wrote in a 2025 brief. “Although the construction of data centers can create many jobs, those are short lived.” Residents were stunned to hear that another data center was coming to their community, telling local news outlet WSAZ that they felt blindsided. Despite not being located on the former nursery’s site, the fate of the American chestnuts have forced Starwood to address it, too.  I emailed Starwood on Oct. 8 asking if its campus threatened the trees. “I checked, and that grove isn’t on Starwood’s land,” a spokesperson told me. Sometime after Sept. 24, according to archives of the site , Project Tamarack added a line to its FAQ section about the grove: “The former Clements State Tree Nursery is a separate property and is not part of the Project Tamarack development site. Project Tamarack has no ownership, control, or management responsibility for the property. Questions regarding the chestnut grove, the former nursery, or the property’s management should be directed to the West Virginia Division of Forestry, which operated the facility prior to its closure in 2021.”  A Farmer Donated Land to Turn into a Park. The City Is Building a Massive Data Center Instead In 1999, a farmer gave away 87 acres of land to a small Texas city to use as a park. The city sold to a data center developer for $10 million. Matthew Gault Nscale also claims that the trees aren’t on land it owns, either — yet. That section of land is technically still under a “plan to purchase agreement.”  “We understand the deep community connection to the former Clements State Tree Nursery site, and we look forward to working closely with the Morrisey Administration—including the Department of Agriculture and Division of Forestry—and The American Chestnut Foundation regarding the American Chestnut trees while responsibly developing the Monarch Compute Campus,” a spokesperson for Nscale told 404 Media. They continued:  “We want to be clear — there was never a plan to bulldoze the nursery or cut down the trees. Nscale does not currently own the former Clements State Tree Nursery but we are under a plan for purchase agreement. Once we own the land, we are focused on how to best care for the trees which, according to a recent assessment by an arborist, suffer from blight and adverse health conditions. We have always planned to incorporate the American Chestnut trees into the Monarch Compute Campus. As construction progresses, we will work closely with professional arborists and experts to determine how best to preserve and integrate them, covering all costs.” Nscale Senior Vice President Pete Hollis told West Virginia Public Broadcasting : “There’s never been a plan to and there will never be a plan to bulldoze or cut down the trees.”  On October 10, Morrisey announced that the trees would eventually be moved, framing this as a way to appease everyone. “Under the preservation plan, the existing trees will be relocated to a more suitable environment within the property, potentially as part of an arboretum or integrated landscaping. That work is scheduled for late 2027, during the trees' dormant season, under professional arborist supervision,” the governor’s office wrote in a press release . Amy Metheny, a forest pathologist for the West Virginia American Chestnut Foundation, told WCHS-TV that relocating the trees would inevitably kill them. “It’s my professional opinion that if the trees were moved they would die within two to five years,” she said. I asked Morrisey’s office if they’re aware that experts say the trees will die if moved. A spokesperson for Morrisey’s office replied:  “We are aware of the concerns about transplanting and have discussed them directly with a member of the West Virginia chapter of The American Chestnut Foundation. The West Virginia Department of Agriculture’s assessment found that the trees are expected to continue dying under current site conditions. It also found that relocating chestnut clumps with proper care may improve their health, although some losses are expected. “Mature chestnut trees from the same original source as the Clements planting are growing in and producing nuts in Tyler County. Approximately 500 nuts from those trees are expected to be used for additional planting to support continued restoration efforts. “The company has said relocation remains its plan and that it will cover the cost. The property is subject to a legally binding purchase option signed in 2023 by the previous administration. We are working with the company and conservation experts to help secure the best possible preservation outcome. Specific questions about those relocation plans should be directed to the company.” Much of the information floating around about the future of the grove — including the claims of looming bulldozers, the timeline for the actual threat to the trees, the “not it” statements between both data center projects, and the governor’s promises — has been a game of rumors and conflicting information. A representative for Goldberry Grove declined to provide an on-the-record source for their claims of a November 1 deadline, or the bulldozer claims. Illustration: Isa Heller / Spumoni Cooperative for 404 Media But the attention turned to an otherwise largely overlooked and tragically rare tree species has stirred up the kind of public action that data center developers around the country have had to contend with when they want to throw miles of humming warehouses up in communities. On October 20, the West Virginia DEP hosted an in-person public comment session about Monarch’s air quality analysis and permitting, with a virtual meeting to come on October 29. The campus’s environmental impact could extend beyond the handful of trees at Clements, according to documents filed with the DEP. The Charleston Gazette-Mail reported , based on those documents: “Construction activities would result in permanent impacts to over 8,400 linear feet of streams and over 1.7 acres of wetlands on one permit and over 5,900 linear feet of streams and more than 26 acres of wetlands on the other, according to the applications.” In addition to being overwhelmingly unpopular with the communities where they’re built, and despite the trillions of dollars dumped into their development, data center projects and the industry at large around the world are starting to flounder. Australia’s NextDC AI data center operator’s shares dropped 40 percent on Wednesday after the company cited power delays and local pushback. Last week, Microsoft pulled out of its deal with Nscale’s Essex-based campus, following reports that the project might not be able to receive a power supply until 2030. Local community opposition to data centers has spurred legislation that’s slowed or halted these projects around the country, with some, including Microsoft in Wisconsin , canceling projects outright following petitions and protests.  Sam Cole is writing from the far reaches of the internet, about sexuality, the adult industry, online culture, and AI. She's the author of How Sex Changed the Internet and the Internet Changed Sex. More from Samantha Cole • •

articles.title: Chinese Megastudios Deploy Immersive Virtual Production Stages to Monetize Tourism and Film
articles.content: At China’s Biggest Studio Complex, Tourists Pay to Play the Lead As AI and funding cuts reduce live-action shoots, tourist packages provide work for crews and give visitors a finished two-minute ultrashort drama of their own. By Fan Yiying Oct 21, 2026 # tourism ZHEJIANG, East China — At China’s largest film and television production base, veteran director Zheng Zhongfu was taking his two leads through a confrontation between a prince and his wronged wife. “In my previous life, you gouged out my heart and left me to die in the wilderness,” he recited, showing them how to deliver the line and where to look. “In this life, I will take back everything that belongs to me.” Qi Kexin and his wife listened closely. But once the cameras rolled, they caught each other’s eye and burst into laughter, forcing Zheng to call cut. Again. “The emotion has to land … your gaze has to focus,” he reminded them. “Whatever you do, don’t laugh. Let’s go again.” Qi, 48, and his wife were tourists at Hengdian World Studios in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, where visitors can pay 388 yuan ($60) per person to star in a short drama of their own. Qi had booked the shoot on a whim after spotting the experience on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok. The package includes costumes, makeup, and filming, with studio performers filling the supporting roles. Visitors spend about an hour in makeup and on set, sometimes longer if they add scenes or need additional coaching. Two days later, they receive a finished two-minute drama with a complete storyline. Earlier tourist shoots required groups of three to five and at least two hours, said Wu Yizhuo, who oversees the service at Hengdian World Studios. “Individual tourists with packed schedules found that hard to accept.” His team developed shorter shoots that a single visitor could book. Visitors can now choose from nearly 30 scripts written by staff screenwriters, drawing on themes from Chinese social media and the country’s booming ultrashort drama industry , including palace intrigue, martial arts fantasy, and romances featuring domineering CEOs. Wu’s team asks visitors whether they want to play a hero or a villain. Most choose villains as a way to relieve stress, he said, with “satisfying revenge” stories especially in demand. Amateur hour Qi chose a palace intrigue script in which he plays a prince who wants to divorce his wife for another woman. His real-life wife plays the wronged spouse, who turns the tables on him with an emperor’s order and a sword. After a nervous start, the pair began to settle into their roles as Zheng coached their dialogue and movements. Their sleeve flicks and sword draws became more assured. “You nailed it!” he called from behind the camera after one take. By the time the shoot wrapped, Qi had a new respect for professional actors. “You have to memorize lines, vary your tone, and add emotion. You can’t attend to everything at once,” he said. “Actors really have it hard. It truly takes skill,” Qi added. “We’re just playing around — we’re far behind the professionals.” Zheng had spent years directing trained actors before he began filming tourists in Hengdian this summer. He breaks difficult lines into smaller pieces, sometimes splitting a sentence across three shots to ease the pressure on visitors, and aims to finish filming in about 30 minutes. Professional crews are serious and not particularly cheerful while filming, Zheng said. With tourists, the focus is on participation and keeping the set lively. “They may not care much about the final film’s quality. The main thing is to come here and be happy.” Zheng is open to visitors adding scenes or lines, or switching into dialect. “As long as the final film works well, it’s fine,” he said. “The more drama there is, the more fully they perform — and the more they share it on social media.” On the day Sixth Tone visited Hengdian, Zheng moved straight from Qi’s shoot to his next performer, Zhang Zhongfeng. The 58-year-old farm owner had driven more than 2,000 kilometers from the southwestern Sichuan province with her daughter for the experience. She had never acted and was nervous when she learned her daughter had booked a shoot for her. Zhang chose palace intrigue, and Zheng tailored a role to her age and temperament. Once filming began, her commanding presence surprised him. Onlookers mistook her for one of the studio performers. Her daughter, Su Jing, 35, filmed a princess scene at another set the next day. “It’s a bit more complicated than filming yourself with a phone, but much simpler than a big movie — no huge number of lines to memorize, and staff guide you throughout,” she said. “It’s like an upgraded version of travel photography.” Zheng said the experience was drawing growing numbers of visitors, particularly during holidays. Nearly 3,000 people have taken part since the package launched in July. Around 2010, Hengdian mainly hosted big-budget films and large TV productions with long shooting schedules, Wu, who oversees the tourist service, recalled. Before one production finished, the next was already booked. “Vertical-screen short dramas have since become more common, while large productions have declined,” he said. In recent months, cheaper AI production and cuts in platform financing have reduced live-action shoots. In Hengdian, the weekly average number of filming crews reportedly fell nearly 25% year on year in the first half of 2026. On peak days, Wu’s team handles 30 to 40 groups of tourists. When its regular staff cannot cover the bookings, the studio calls in local part-time workers. Zheng films tourist dramas as a member of one such outsourced team. Giovana Velasco, a tourist from Peru, first visited Hengdian last year, when the experience wasn’t available, she recalled. After spotting it on Trip.com this year, she booked a shoot and chose to play a rejected daughter seeking revenge. She rehearsed lines in Chinese, Spanish, and English, battled nerves and laughter, and sometimes relied on body language to stay in character. Her shoot took twice as long as those of Chinese visitors. She is already planning another trip to play a scheming sister and surprise her TikTok followers. A Shanghai tourist surnamed Xia chose a scene from the 2011 Chinese period drama “Empresses in the Palace” in which her character slaps a maid who has struck her first. She booked the shoot after seeing influencers perform in Hengdian on social media. “Just for fun, out of curiosity,” she joked. articles.title: South African Visa Digitization Paralysis Traps High-Skilled Tech Workers at Union Buildings
articles.content: Scapegoating migrants won’t fix a deliberately broken Home Affairs system or create jobs. South Africa needs real administrative leadership, not political theatre. By Bafana Khumalo 21 Oct 2026 0 Bafana Khumalo is a human rights activist and co-founder of Sonke Gender Justice. Dive Deeper Speed Read Listen Dive Deeper , which presents the writer's personal point of view. The views expressed are those of the author/authors and do not necessarily represent the views of Daily Maverick. Every few months, South Africa undergoes a similar ritual. A clinic is overwhelmed in Hillbrow. A township business is looted. A truck is burnt on the N3. A mother in Limpopo gives birth on the floor because the maternity ward is full. And immediately, we point at the foreigner. Then politicians arrive with loudhailers. One party promises to close the border. Another promises to give everyone documents. Another promises to deport 12 million people in 12 months – a logistical impossibility that would require a fleet of planes we don’t have. And after the march, after the speech, nothing changes. The border remains porous, Home Affairs remains broken and the poor – both South African and foreign – continue to fight over crumbs at the margins of the mainstream economy. The immigration challenge in South Africa is real. But what it demonstrates above all is a massive, sustained failure of political leadership. 1. We have confused control with cruelty South Africa has one of the most progressive constitutions in the world. It promises rights to “everyone”, not just citizens. We signed the UN Refugee Convention . We are a member of the African Union, which preaches Pan-Africanism . But we have a Home Affairs system that is deliberately dysfunctional. Try to obtain asylum in South Africa today. You will queue from 3am at the Desmond Tutu Refugee Reception Office in Marabastad. You will be told the system is offline. You will be issued a Section 22 permit that expires after six months, requiring you to return again and again. Employers do not recognise it. Banks do not recognise it. Police tear it up at roadblocks and ask for a bribe. The result is predictable: People who should be documented become undocumented because the state makes it impossible to stay documented. Then the state calls them “illegal” and raids them. This is not border control. This is manufactured illegality. And it serves a purpose: It creates a pool of cheap, exploitable labour that can be blamed when things go wrong. Political leadership has failed to fix Home Affairs because a broken Home Affairs is politically useful. 2. We don’t tell the truth about the economy The uncomfortable truth politicians won’t say on a podium is this: South Africa’s economy needs migrants and has needed them for 150 years. Our mines were built on Mozambican, Basotho and Malawian labour. Our farms in Limpopo and the De Doorns valley run on Zimbabwean labour . Our hospitals in rural Eastern Cape are staffed by Cuban and Nigerian doctors because South African doctors won’t go there. Our restaurants in Cape Town and Sandton rely on Malawian waiters. Many township spaza shops are sustained by Ethiopian and Somali entrepreneurs who wake up at 4am, extend credit to customers, and sell in small units where large retailers often do not. Numerous studies, including by the World Bank and UCT, show that migrants are net contributors to GDP, not job takers. They create jobs. They pay VAT. They don’t qualify for R350 SRD grants. But instead of building a managed labour migration system – like Canada’s points system or a proper SADC work visa regime – we have left it to smugglers. We have a 3,000km border with Zimbabwe, Mozambique, Botswana, Namibia, Lesotho and Eswatini, fenced so poorly that some holes are wide enough to drive a taxi through. The Border Management Authority has 2,600 staff for the entire border and a vacancy rate of 75%. We spend more on VIP protection for politicians than on border technology. That is not the failure of the immigrant who crosses at Beitbridge. That is the failure of the state that knew for 30 years the fence was broken and did nothing. 3. We have outsourced governance to mob rule The most dangerous failure is this: When the state fails to provide housing, jobs and healthcare, it allows communities to turn on each other instead of turning on the state. In 2008, 62 foreign nationals were killed in xenophobic attacks . In 2015, seven were killed . In 2019, numerous shops were looted again. In 2021, we watched Operation Dudula rise. In every case, political leaders either quietly fanned the flames or arrived late with condemnation. No mayor has ever lost their job because a clinic ran out of medicine. But a foreign shopkeeper can lose their life for the same reason. This is classic scapegoating. And it works because our leaders have never implemented a coherent integration plan: Where are the community dialogues between local business forums and foreign trader associations? Where is the by-law that allows a South African and an Ethiopian to trade legally without paying a bribe to a councillor? Where is the plan to document spaza shops instead of burning them? Rwanda, with a genocide in its history, has integrated refugees. Kenya hosts 700,000 refugees in Kakuma. South Africa, with one of the continent's most advanced economies, cannot effectively manage 300,000 asylum seekers because it has chosen not to prioritise doing so. What would leadership look like? It would not be open borders. No serious country has open borders. And it would not be mass deportation, which is both immoral and impossible. Leadership would look like four honest things: Fix Home Affairs first. Digitise the asylum process, issue five-year permits that employers can verify and clear the backlog of 300,000 appeals that has accumulated since 2012. Corrupt officials who sell passports must be imprisoned, not just transferred. Introduce a real SADC work visa. Let a Zimbabwean teacher come legally for three years to teach mathematics in Lusikisiki, pay tax and then go home – instead of paying R5,000 to a smuggler and living in fear. Remittances already prop up the region; let us formalise the system. Enforce labour law for everyone. If a farmer pays a Zimbabwean R150 a day below minimum wage, jail the farmer, not just deport the worker. Exploitation thrives because enforcement is selective. Stop using foreigners as a distraction . Every time a politician says “foreigners are taking jobs” without showing us their plan for jobs, youth unemployment and the energy crisis, he is telling you he has no plan. The conundrum is not that people move. People have always moved. The conundrum is that in 30 years of democracy, we have not built a state capable of managing movement with dignity, legality and common sense. The border is not the problem. The Union Buildings are.
